title: Four thoughts that turn the mind
hook: precious human life, death, karma, the faults of samsara

segments.voice: Yesterday: lungta, wheels and flags, and your line, the wind carries it. Did you do one kind thing nobody will credit you for? Day three hundred eight, the end of the week.

Most people change direction only after a jolt. A doctor's call. A birthday with a zero on the end. A friend who was fine last month, and isn't. For a week or two, everything looks different: what matters, what doesn't, how you want to spend your hours. Then the feeling fades and the old grooves take over. Tibetan teachers noticed this long ago, and they built the jolt into the very start of the path, on purpose, so it wouldn't depend on bad news. Today: four thoughts that turn the mind.
screen: `A DOCTOR'S CALL. A BIRTHDAY.` → `EVERYTHING LOOKS DIFFERENT.` → `THEN THE OLD GROOVES RETURN.`

segments.voice: In Tibetan practice, these four reflections come before everything else, and people return to them for a lifetime. The first is precious human life. Tibetan teachers borrow an image the Buddha gives in the Pali discourses: a blind turtle in the great ocean rises to the surface once every hundred years, and a wooden yoke with one hole drifts on the waves. The turtle will put its head through that hole, the Buddha says, sooner than a being who has fallen into the lower realms will win back a human birth. So this life, with the time and freedom to learn anything at all, is rare. The second is death and impermanence. Death is certain; its time is not. The third is karma: actions have results, and the small ones add up. The fourth is the faults of samsara, the round of birth and death: even the good parts don't last, and chasing them never quite satisfies. The twelfth-century teacher Gampopa taught all four in a famous book, and the preliminary practices set them in this order, which matters. First you see how lucky you are. Then how short the time is. Then how much your actions count. Then that more chasing won't fix it. Put together, the mind turns, like a boat swinging around in the current, toward the path. Now look back at the week. For a while. The question is still open. Virtue, calm, wisdom. The elders' day. Then the climb: the diamond vehicle. The jewel in the lotus. The wind carries it. And today: turn the mind.
screen: `PRECIOUS HUMAN LIFE.` · `DEATH IS CERTAIN, ITS TIME IS NOT.` · `ACTIONS HAVE RESULTS.` · `CHASING NEVER QUITE SATISFIES.` · then, large: `TURN THE MIND.`

segments.voice: For this sit, choose one of the four and stay with it. If you choose precious human life, picture the turtle and the yoke, and then look at your own hands: here you are, with time to sit. If you choose death, rest in the thought that this breath is one of a limited number. Don't push toward a feeling. Just let the thought sit beside you, the way you'd sit beside a friend. When the mind wanders, return to the one you chose. The bell holds the time.
Gampopa. The twelfth-century teacher who taught the four thoughts in a famous book: precious human life, death, karma, and the faults of samsara.
Your line: turn the mind. Today, when the day pulls you into an old groove, pause and ask: given how rare and short this is, what would I choose instead? Day three hundred eight.

howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists often recite and reflect on the four thoughts at the start of each practice session, and they form the first part of the preliminary practices (ngöndro) taught in all the Tibetan schools.

pairs: certain, but its time is not

the Buddha uses it to show how rare a human birth is.
the four thoughts are for advanced students only

the order of the four doesn't matter
luck first, then urgency, then care, then seeing that chasing won't fix it.

fork.setup: you've just heard that human life is precious and death's timing unknown. a Tibetan teacher asks what you'll do with that. which answer fits the four thoughts?
options: panic and try to do everything at once.
let it turn the mind toward what matters, steadily.
fork.reveal: the four thoughts aren't meant to frighten but to turn the mind, like a boat in the current, toward the path.

original.note: Tibetan blo ldog rnam bzhi: blo (mind) + ldog (turn back) + rnam bzhi (the four): the four thoughts that turn the mind.

trapdoor: what you thought: gloomy thoughts to make you feel bad.
what it means: four reflections that turn the mind toward the path: luck, urgency, care, and seeing through the chase.

what a scholar hears: Gampopa's Jewel Ornament of Liberation teaches all four early on, after buddha-nature; as the 'common' preliminaries of ngöndro they are shared by Nyingma, Kagyu, Sakya and Gelug alike.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 129, Balapandita Sutta (the blind turtle and the yoke)
Gampopa, Jewel Ornament of Liberation (the four thoughts)

notes: The turtle simile also appears at SN 56.47–48; paraphrased. In the Pali version the Buddha compares it to a fool regaining a human birth after falling to lower realms; the simplified framing here should be checked.
The four thoughts are presented in different orders in some texts (e.g. the Kagyu formulation); confirm the order used.
Gampopa (1079–1153) and the Jewel Ornament's structure: confirm.
